---
title: "Sex chromosomes and mtDNA"
output: html_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

Most analyses in population genetics assume diploid loci, but the ploidy of
a locus on a sex chromosome depends on the sex of the individual. In XY
systems (e.g. mammals), males have one X and one Y, and females two X and
no Y; in ZW systems (e.g. birds), females have one Z and one W. The
mitochondrial genome (mtDNA) is haploid in everyone. Only the
pseudo-autosomal regions (PAR) of the sex chromosomes behave like
autosomes. This article shows how `tidypopgen` deals with these loci:

1. how it recognises sex chromosomes and mtDNA;
2. how it stores the genotypes of hemizygous individuals;
3. how to check the recorded sex of individuals;
4. which analyses use autosomes only;
5. how sex chromosomes are written to PLINK and VCF files.

`tidypopgen` follows PLINK's conventions throughout.

## The data

We simulate a small dataset of 10 females and 10 males, with 50 loci on an
autosome, 100 on the X chromosome, 10 on Y and 5 on mtDNA. As in PLINK, the
genotypes of males on X and Y (and of everyone on mtDNA), which have a
single allele, are stored as homozygotes (0 or 2).

```{r data, message=FALSE}
library(tidypopgen)
set.seed(42)
n_females <- 10
n_males <- 10
male <- rep(c(FALSE, TRUE), c(n_females, n_males))
# diploid genotypes, and haploid ones stored as homozygotes
diploid <- function(p, n) t(replicate(n, rbinom(length(p), 2, p)))
haploid <- function(p, n) 2 * t(replicate(n, rbinom(length(p), 1, p)))
p_x <- runif(100, 0.1, 0.9)
x <- matrix(NA, length(male), 100)
x[!male, ] <- diploid(p_x, n_females)
x[male, ] <- haploid(p_x, n_males)
y <- matrix(NA, length(male), 10)
y[male, ] <- haploid(runif(10, 0.2, 0.8), n_males)
geno <- cbind(
  diploid(runif(50, 0.1, 0.9), length(male)),
  x,
  y,
  haploid(runif(5, 0.2, 0.8), length(male))
)
loci <- data.frame(
  name = paste0("snp", 1:165),
  chromosome = rep(c("1", "X", "Y", "MT"), c(50, 100, 10, 5)),
  position = c(1:50, 1:100, 1:10, 1:5) * 1000,
  genetic_dist = 0,
  allele_ref = "A",
  allele_alt = "G"
)
sex_gt <- gen_tibble(geno,
  loci = loci,
  indiv_meta = data.frame(
    id = paste0("ind", 1:20),
    population = "pop1",
    sex = ifelse(male, "male", "female")
  ),
  backingfile = tempfile("sex_chromosomes_"),
  quiet = TRUE
)
sex_gt
```

The sex of individuals is stored in the column `sex`. It is read from PLINK
`.fam` and `.ped` files and from EIGENSOFT `.ind` files; for VCF files, which
do not record it, add it with `mutate()` or a join with the metadata.

## Recognising sex chromosomes and mtDNA

Chromosomes named "X", "Y", "Z", "W", "XY", "PAR1", "PAR2", "MT" or "M" (in
any case, with or without "chr") are recognised from their names:

```{r types}
gt_chromosome_types(sex_gt)
```

Numbers are never recognised, as their meaning depends on the species: PLINK
codes the human X chromosome as 23, but chromosome 23 is an autosome in many
other species. Declare them with `gt_set_chromosome_types()`, e.g. with
PLINK's human codes (`chr_set = "human"`, i.e. 23 to 26 for X, Y, XY and MT),
the codes of another number of autosomes (`chr_set = 38` for a dog), or
chromosome by chromosome (`types = c("23" = "X")`). The pseudo-autosomal
regions of the human X chromosome are declared with `par = "b37"` (or "b36"
and "b38"), with the boundaries of PLINK's `--split-x`.

`loci_chromosome_types()` gives the type of each locus, e.g. to keep the
autosomes only:

```{r autosomes}
sex_gt %>%
  select_loci_if(loci_chromosome_types(genotypes) == "autosome") %>%
  count_loci()
```

## Reading hemizygous genotypes

In a VCF, the genotype of a male on X is often haploid (e.g. `1` rather than
`1/1`). `gen_tibble()`, `gt_merge_vcfs()` and `gt_concat_vcfs()` store a
haploid genotype of a diploid individual as a homozygote (0 or 2), as
PLINK does, so that the same data give the same genotypes whether they are
read from a VCF or a PLINK file. Haploid genotypes on chromosomes recognised
as sex chromosomes or mtDNA do not set the ploidy of individuals: a VCF that
starts with the X chromosome still gives diploid males.

## Checking the sex of individuals

Males have a single X, so all their genotypes on X are homozygous, and their
inbreeding coefficient F on X is close to 1, whereas that of females is close
to 0. `indiv_sex_check()` estimates the sex of each individual from its F, as
PLINK's `--check-sex`, and compares it with the recorded sex. Let us record
two individuals with the wrong sex:

```{r sex_check}
sex_gt$sex[c(1, 20)] <- c("male", "female")
indiv_sex_check(sex_gt)
```

The two individuals are flagged as "PROBLEM", and so is `ind2`: with only
100 loci on X, its F falls between the largest F of a female (0.2) and the
smallest F of a male (0.8), so its sex is unknown. With `ycount = TRUE`, the
number of genotypes on Y is also used (females should have none).

```{r sex_check_y}
indiv_sex_check(sex_gt, ycount = TRUE, min_male_ycount = 5) %>%
  dplyr::filter(status == "PROBLEM")
```

## Analyses use autosomes only

Most analyses assume that loci are on diploid autosomes. On the X
chromosome, males are homozygous, which looks like inbreeding and adds the
sex of individuals to the structure of the data. As PLINK does (e.g. for
KING), the functions that pool loci into statistics of individuals, pairs of
individuals or populations, the PCA, and the inputs of ADMIXTURE, sNMF and
ADMIXTOOLS 2 use autosomal loci only, and say how many loci they left out:

```{r analyses}
het <- indiv_het_obs(sex_gt)
pca <- gt_pca(sex_gt, k = 2)
```

The documentation of `gt_set_chromosome_types()` lists these functions. To
include a sex chromosome or mtDNA in them, declare it as an autosome:

```{r declare_autosome}
sex_gt %>%
  gt_set_chromosome_types(types = c(X = "autosome")) %>%
  gt_pca(k = 2)
```

The functions that return one value per locus (e.g. `loci_alt_freq()` or
`loci_hwe()`) use all loci, but do not yet treat males as haploid: on X,
they count two alleles per male, and their HWE tests fail. Select the loci
of the types you need before using them.

## Writing sex chromosomes

`gt_as_vcf()` writes the genotypes of males on X and Y (of females on Z and
W), and of everyone on mtDNA, as haploid genotypes. A heterozygous genotype
of a hemizygous individual (e.g. a genotyping error, or a male in the
pseudo-autosomal region if it was not declared) is written as missing, as
PLINK treats such genotypes as missing.

```{r write_vcf}
vcf_file <- gt_as_vcf(sex_gt, file = tempfile(fileext = ".vcf"))
vcf_lines <- readLines(vcf_file)
# the first genotypes of a locus on X (individuals 1 and 20 are recorded with
# the wrong sex)
x_line <- strsplit(vcf_lines[grep("^X\t", vcf_lines)[1]], "\t")[[1]]
x_line[10:29]
```

`gt_as_plink()` writes the names of the chromosomes, or, with
`chromosomes_as_int = TRUE`, PLINK's integer codes (23 to 26 for X, Y, XY and
MT in humans, or the codes of the number of autosomes declared with
`chr_set`).
